facts.statement: The genus Martinavis was named by Cyril A. Walker, Eric Buffetaut, and Gareth J. Dyke in 2007.
facts.quote: It was named by Cyril A. Walker, Eric Buffetaut and Gareth J. Dyke in 2007

facts.statement: Martinavis lived during the late Cretaceous period in what is now southern France, North America, and Salta Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: Martinavis is a genus of enantiornithine birds which existed in what is now southern France, North America and Salta Province, Argentina during the late Cretaceous period

facts.statement: Martinavis is classified as a genus of enantiornithine birds.
facts.quote: Martinavis is a genus of enantiornithine birds

facts.statement: The type species M. cruzyensis is known from a complete right humerus found in the Grès à Reptiles Formation of France.
facts.quote: M. cruzyensis is known from the holotype ACAP-M 1957, a complete uncrushed right humerus, recovered from the Massecaps locality, Cruzy, which is in a Campanian/Maastrichtian-stage deposits in the Grès à Reptiles Formation of France

facts.statement: M. vincei is known from a complete left humerus and a distal left humerus fragment found in the Lecho Formation of Argentina.
facts.quote: A second species, M. vincei is known from the holotype PVL 4054, a complete left humerus and from the associated paratype PVL 4059, a distal end of left humerus, recovered from the El Brete locality (Maastrichtian age), Lecho Formation of Argentina

facts.statement: M. vincei reached a length of 51 cm, a hip height of 22.3 cm, and a weight of 1.8 kg.
facts.quote: PVL 4054 and PVL 4059 indicate the animals with a length of 51 cm, hip height of 22.3 cm, and weight of 1.8 kg

facts.statement: M. saltariensis was the second largest species, measuring 44.2 cm in length, 19.3 cm in hip height, and weighing 1.2 kg.
facts.quote: M. saltariensis is the second largest species, with a length of 44.2 cm, hip height of 19.3 cm, and weight of 1.2 kg

facts.statement: M. whetstonei was a very small species, at most half the size of M. vincei.
facts.quote: M. whetstonei was a diminutive version of M. vincei, being at most half its size

facts.statement: Three additional species—M. minor, M. saltariensis, and M. whetstonei—were named in 2009 from the same location as M. vincei.
facts.quote: In 2009, three additional species were named from the same location as M. vincei: M. minor is known from the holotype PVL 4046, a distally imperfect right humerus; M. saltariensis is known from the holotype PVL 4025, an incomplete left humerus, lacking the median ridge; M. whetstonei is known from the holotype PVL 4028, a distally imperfect left humerus

facts.statement: M. vincei was the largest species from the El Brete locality, reaching a size comparable to the large Enantiornis.
facts.quote: M. vincei is the largest of the El Brete taxa, approaching its huge (by enantiornithine standards), sympatric and coeval Enantiornis in size

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that some El Brete Martinavis specimens might actually be the same species as other enantiornithines previously described from leg bones.
facts.quote: As few elements are known from El Brete Martinavis, it might be the same species as one of the other enantiornithines of that locality which were described earlier based on leg bones

facts.statement: It is debated whether some Martinavis specimens should be synonymized with Yungavolucris, a foot-propelled swimmer, which would explain the genus's presence in marine environments.
facts.quote: As Yungavolucris is assumed to be a foot-propelled swimmer however the synonymity of at least some Martinavis specimens with it could explain the genus' prevalence in marine biomes

facts.statement: Martinavis lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

rejected.quote: This species reached 42.7 cm in length, 18.7 cm in hip height and 1.1 kg in weight
